His words, exalted is He: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾ ﴿that run and hide﴾ ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾ ﴿and by the dawn when it breathes⁠﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the word of a noble messenger﴾ ﴿endowed with power, with rank before the Lord of the Throne﴾ ﴿obeyed there and trustworthy﴾ ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾ ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾ ﴿And he is not withholding of the unseen﴾ ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ ﴿So where are you going?﴾ ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ ﴿for whoever among you wishes to go straight﴾ ﴿And you will not wish unless God wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

His words, exalted is He: "So I do not swear" (fa-la uqsimu). Either the "la" is superfluous (za'idah), or it is a response to what the Quraysh said in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and their claim that he was a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and similar things. Then God, exalted is He, swore by "the receding, running, and hiding" (al-khunnas al-jawari al-kunnas). The majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin) said that these are the seven planets: the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, Mercury, Mars, Venus, and Jupiter.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said that what is meant is the five (planets), excluding the Sun and the Moon. This is because these stars "recede" (takhnis) in their course, meaning they retreat as far as the eye can see, and they "run" (jiwar) in the sky. Ya'qub read the yā' in "al-jawari" in pause, while the rest omitted it. They "hide" (takunis) in their constellations, meaning they conceal themselves.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said that what is meant is all the stars, because they recede and hide by day when they are concealed.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, Jabir ibn Zayd, and a group of exegetes said that what is meant by "the receding, running, and hiding" is the wild oxen (baqar al-wahsh), because they do these actions in their kunnas, which are the places they take shelter in, such as trees, caves, and the like.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak said that they are the gazelles (zaba'). These scholars took "khunnas" to be a description of the noses, since the gazelles are characterized by it, and likewise the wild oxen. From this is the verse of the poet:

"Other than a white falcon or a gazelle of the desert, / Plump, with a flat nose and twin..."

"And the night breathed out" (wa 'as'asa al-layl): in the language, it means when the darkness is not fully established. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said that it refers to its coming (iqbal), and with this the oath was made. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, Mujahid, and Qatadah said that it refers to its departure (idbar), and with this the oath was made. This is supported by His words after it: "and by the dawn when it breathes," so the two are like connected states. The verse of 'Alqamah ibn Qurt supports this:

"Until, when the dawn breathed for it / and its night withdrew from it and departed⁠..."

Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad said: God swore by its coming and its departure together. Al-Khalil said: It is said, "'as'asa al-layl" and "sa'sa'a" when it comes and goes.

"Tanaffasa al-subh" means that its light spread and expanded. 'Ilwan ibn Qays said:

"And a dark night whose dawn breathed upon them, / after they had thought it would never breathe."

The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the Qur'an. "The noble messenger," according to the majority of people, is Jibril (peace be upon him). Others said it is Muhammad (peace be upon him) in all the verses. The first opinion is more sound. The word "karim" (noble) in this verse implies the removal of blameworthy qualities. Then He described him with the power that God granted him.

People differed about the connection of His words, "before the Lord of the Throne." Some interpreters connected it to His words, "endowed with power," while others said the sentence is complete at His words, "endowed with power," and the adverbial phrase is connected to "makin" (established), meaning: he has standing and elevation.

His words, "obeyed there and trustworthy," mean: his word is accepted, he is believed in what he says, and he is entrusted with what he conveys and delivers of revelation and carrying out commands. Abu Ja'far read "thamma" with a damma on the tha'. God mentioned Himself through its attribution to His Throne, to alert to the greatness of His dominion.

The exegetes agreed that His words, "And your companion," refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in "ra'ahu" refers to Jibril (peace be upon him). This vision happened after the event of the cave of Hira, when he saw him on a chair between heaven and earth. It was also said that this vision was when he saw him at Sidrat al-Muntaha during the Isra'. That place was called "horizon" metaphorically. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a second vision in Medina, but this is not it. God described the horizon as "clear" because it was in the east, from where the sun rises, as Qatadah said. Also, every horizon is in complete clarity.

His words, "And he is not withholding (ḍanin) of the unseen": with the ḍad, meaning "miserly," i.e., he does not hold back from it, and he does not fail to convey what he has been told, nor is he stingy as a soothsayer does until he is given his payment (hulwan). With the ḍad, it is so in all the mushafs, according to what al-Tabari said. It is the recitation of Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and a large group. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'A'ishah, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Ibn Jubayr, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Muslim, Ibn Jundub, Mujahid, and others read "ẓanin" with the ẓa', meaning "accused" (muttaham). This in meaning is like the description of him as "trustworthy." It was also said that it means "weak in strength," from the expression "bi'r ẓanun," when a well has little water. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading with the ẓa' with imalah (a slight inclination in pronunciation), because the Quraysh did not accuse Muhammad (ﷺ) of withholding what he brought; rather, they denied him, so it was said: "He is not accused."

Then God negated from the Qur'an that it is the speech of a devil, as the Quraysh claimed that Muhammad was a soothsayer. "Rajim" means expelled and stoned, with shooting stars, the curse, and other things.

His words, "So where are you going?", are a reproach and a confirmation, in the sense of: where is the way out for anyone from these realities? "Dhikr" (reminder) here is a verbal noun meaning remembrance. Then God specified for whoever wishes to be upright with the mention, as an honor, an alert, and a mention, because they acquire the actions of uprightness. Then God explained that a person's acquisition in general, whether in uprightness or otherwise, only happens together with God's creation and His bringing into being of faith in a person's breast. It is narrated that when His words, "for whoever among you wishes to go straight," were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "This is a matter left to us. If we wish, we go straight, and if we do not wish, we do not go straight." So this was revealed: ﴿And you will not wish unless God wills﴾.

In a hadith: "God says: O son of Adam, you wish and I wish, and you toil in what you wish, but nothing happens except what I wish."

The commentary of Surah [al-Takwir] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Some interpreters connected it to His words, "endowed with power," while others said the sentence is complete at His words, "endowed with power," and the adverbial phrase is connected to "makin" (established), meaning: he has standing and elevation.

His words, "obeyed there and trustworthy," mean: his word is accepted, he is believed in what he says, and he is entrusted with what he conveys and delivers of revelation and carrying out commands. Abu Ja'far read "thamma" with a damma on the tha'. God mentioned Himself through its attribution to His Throne, to alert to the greatness of His dominion.

The exegetes agreed that His words, "And your companion," refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in "ra'ahu" refers to Jibril (peace be upon him). This vision happened after the event of the cave of Hira, when he saw him on a chair between heaven and earth. It was also said that this vision was when he saw him at Sidrat al-Muntaha during the Isra'. That place was called "horizon" metaphorically. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a second vision in Medina, but this is not it. God described the horizon as "clear" because it was in the east, from where the sun rises, as Qatadah said. Also, every horizon is in complete clarity.

His words, "And he is not withholding (ḍanin) of the unseen": with the ḍad, meaning "miserly," i.e., he does not hold back from it, and he does not fail to convey what he has been told, nor is he stingy as a soothsayer does until he is given his payment (hulwan). With the ḍad, it is so in all the mushafs, according to what al-Tabari said. It is the recitation of Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and a large group. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'A'ishah, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Ibn Jubayr, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Muslim, Ibn Jundub, Mujahid, and others read "ẓanin" with the ẓa', meaning "accused" (muttaham). This in meaning is like the description of him as "trustworthy." It was also said that it means "weak in strength," from the expression "bi'r ẓanun," when a well has little water. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading with the ẓa' with imalah (a slight inclination in pronunciation), because the Quraysh did not accuse Muhammad (ﷺ) of withholding what he brought; rather, they denied him, so it was said: "He is not accused."

Then God negated from the Qur'an that it is the speech of a devil, as the Quraysh claimed that Muhammad was a soothsayer. "Rajim" means expelled and stoned, with shooting stars, the curse, and other things.

His words, "So where are you going?", are a reproach and a confirmation, in the sense of: where is the way out for anyone from these realities? "Dhikr" (reminder) here is a verbal noun meaning remembrance. Then God specified for whoever wishes to be upright with the mention, as an honor, an alert, and a mention, because they acquire the actions of uprightness. Then God explained that a person's acquisition in general, whether in uprightness or otherwise, only happens together with God's creation and His bringing into being of faith in a person's breast. It is narrated that when His words, "for whoever among you wishes to go straight," were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "This is a matter left to us. If we wish, we go straight, and if we do not wish, we do not go straight." So this was revealed: ﴿And you will not wish unless God wills﴾.

In a hadith: "God says: O son of Adam, you wish and I wish, and you toil in what you wish, but nothing happens except what I wish."

The commentary of Surah [al-Takwir] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-Takwir (81), verses 15–29:

His words, exalted is He: "So I do not swear" (fa-la uqsimu). Either the "la" is superfluous (za'idah), or it is a response to what the Quraysh said in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and their claim that he was a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and similar things. Then God, exalted is He, swore by "the receding, running, and hiding" (al-khunnas al-jawari al-kunnas). The majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin) said that these are the seven planets: the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, Mercury, Mars, Venus, and Jupiter.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said that what is meant is the five (planets), excluding the Sun and the Moon. This is because these stars "recede" (takhnis) in their course, meaning they retreat as far as the eye can see, and they "run" (jiwar) in the sky. Ya'qub read the yā' in "al-jawari" in pause, while the rest omitted it. They "hide" (takunis) in their constellations, meaning they conceal themselves.

"Other than a white falcon or a gazelle of the desert, / Plump, with a flat nose and twin..."

"Tanaffasa al-subh" means that its light spread and expanded. 'Ilwan ibn Qays said:

"And a dark night whose dawn breathed upon them, / after they had thought it would never breathe."
